output.title: What seasonality hides in one recurring workflow
output.body:
Seasonality can hide a workflow problem, not just a sales problem. When revenue rises and falls, it is easy to miss the same task repeating all year in the background: customer questions, invoice work, or data cleanup that keeps coming back even when the business feels quiet.

The practical decision is simple: pick one recurring process and ask whether it changes in peak season or just gets harder to notice. If the work is repetitive, has a clear input and output, and you can define what “correct” looks like, it may be a better candidate for automation than a bigger, messier project.

Start with a short list of 2–3 workflows that seasonality tends to bury. Choose the one with the clearest measure, such as delay, error rate, or approval time. Then check whether the task still exists in the slow months, because a workflow that disappears for half the year is usually a poor first bet.

If it does persist, the next step is a free diagnostic: map that workflow end to end, note where the human approval has to stay in place, and test whether a small automation tool like Zapier, Make, or n8n could hand back a human-approved output.

That is often the real question hiding inside seasonality: what is actually changing, and what is simply being covered up by the calendar.
